title: Pauri 37, meaning: grace and truth
hookLine: in the realm of grace dwell the mighty in spirit; in the realm of truth dwells the Formless, beholding all (Japji 37)
last: KARAM KHANDD — THE REALM OF GRACE.

cards: Describe your mother's voice, or your grandfather's laugh, to someone who never heard it. A few words come: warm, a bit low, it cracks at the end. Then the words run out, because they're so much smaller than the thing.
Knowing and telling are different skills, and some things only allow one of them. Two stanzas ago, Saram Khand warned that its matters can't be told.
Pauri 37 climbs to the very top of the Japji's ladder, and there Guru Nanak meets that wall again, harder than before.

teach.h: KARAM KHAND — THE MIGHTY IN SPIRIT.
teach.b: Who lives in the realm of grace? Tithai jodh mahaabal soor: warriors of great strength, heroes, and the Lord, here called Raam, a name the Granth uses for the One who fills everything, is completely present in them.

They neither die nor are deceived, the stanza says, those in whose minds the One lives. Devotees of many worlds dwell there, full of joy, the True One in their hearts. That's the fourth realm, Karam Khand.
Then the fifth, the top of the ladder: sach khandd vasai nirankaar.
In the realm of truth dwells the Formless One. And what does the Formless do there?

teach.h: HE WATCHES, BLESSING WITH A GLANCE.
teach.b: Kar kar vekhai nadar nihaal: creating, He watches over it all, and blesses with a glance. You heard that watching in Pauris 30 and 31; here it's at home.
In Sach Khand there are continents, worlds and universes without end; worlds upon worlds of forms, each moving as the order moves it. He sees, He is delighted, He reflects. And then Nanak stops.
To describe it is as hard as steel. Saar is steel, iron: you could chew on it forever and not bite through. In Pauri 36 the words fell short; here they meet steel.
Some Sikh teachers describe Sach Khand not only as a place after this life but as a state to be touched now, in the heart, when the Formless is near.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 37 describes Karam Khand, the realm of grace, and Sach Khand, the realm of truth where the Formless dwells, and ends with Nanak saying that describing it is as hard as steel.

o: the realm of truth, where the Formless dwells
a paradise earned by good deeds alone
a palace where earthly kings hold court

games.q: what's inside Pauri 37 — tap the pairs.
p: the Formless dwells in truth's realm

s: in the realm of grace dwell warriors of great strength
tithai jodh mahaabal soor: the mighty in spirit, with the One filling them.
in Sach Khand the Formless creates and watches over creation
Pauri 37 says those in the realm of grace die and are deceived like anyone else
the stanza says they neither die nor are deceived, those in whose minds the One lives.

games.q: you've reached the top of the ladder, Sach Khand. you're asked to describe it. what does Nanak do?
o: says telling it is as hard as steel.
says only the yogis can describe it.
games.why: Nanak kathnaa karrarraa saar. the top of the ladder ends with steel, not a map.

practice: Bring to mind the things you're grateful for, one at a time, without describing them: a face, a meal, a morning, a voice. Let each one arrive, feel the thanks, and let it go; if a word comes, let it pass too.
When the list runs out, rest in the thanks itself.

wordCard.voice: Sach Khand. The realm of truth, where the Formless One dwells, creating and watching with a kindly glance. The fifth realm, the top of the ladder, and too hard to tell.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 37: in the realm of truth dwells the Formless.

carryVoice: Your line: hard as steel to tell. Where the words run out, silence is enough. See you tomorrow.
